https://www.barrons.com/articles/cvs-supersize-44b-bond-for-aetna-deal-gets-triple-orders-1520367524 CVS Supersize $44B Bond for Aetna Deal Gets Triple Orders By March 6, 2018 3:18 p.m. ET Text Size Medium Large 
CVS Health (CVS) took advantage of a rare respite in the Treasury's nearly nonstop auctions of notes and bonds to bring its own government-size bond offering of $44 billion of fresh debt to finance its pending acquisition of insurer Aetna (AET). Illustration: Ben Torres/Bloomberg 
The CVS deal had been premarketed to institutional investors for weeks, according to one buy-side professional we spoke with on background. 
Like Treasury auctions, CVS' deal is drawing a similar multiple of bids for the new issues—some $120 billion, according to Andrew Brenner of Natalliance Securities . That would figure to a 2.7 times bid-to-cover ratio, which Uncle Sam would be delighted to receive. That's due to the deal being priced "cheaper" (that is, higher in yield) relative to outstanding CVS issues, according to Mark Grant , chief global strategist of B. Riley FBR and Wunderlich Securities . 
"There was a lot of institutional interest" for CVS, a relatively new and well-thought-of name to the corporate bond market, he says. 
The yields were the main attraction, with the 30-year tranche having a preliminary price equivalent to 195 basis points (1.95 percentage points) above the Treasury 30-year bond, Grant says. Spreads for the 20- and 10-year portions were 180 and 160 basis points, respectively. All have since traded higher in price to narrow those spreads, he adds. (The deal also consists of two- and three-year notes with fixed coupons that convert to floating rates, plus intermediate maturities of five and seven years.) 
The CVS offering had been weighing on the overall market and was responsible at least in part for a backup in yields since Friday, according to Tom Digaloma of Seaport Global Investors. Underwriters of big corporate bond holdings typically hedge their exposure in the Treasury cash or futures market. 
There also is an advantage to a corporate borrower in bringing a massive issue to market. Index funds have to own the credit, regardless of its merits, simply because its size means it comprises a significant percentage of the major bond indexes. This is a major difference between indexing in debt and equity worlds. 
For instance, Apple (AAPL) is the world's largest-capitalization stock and comprises nearly 4% of the SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY), owing to the iPhone maker's commercial and financial success. 
For the iShares iBoxx $ Investment Grade Corporate Bond ETF (LQD), Anheuser-Busch InBev (BUD) is among the top holdings, owning to the brewer's debt-fueled acquisitions. Ditto Verizon Communications (VZ), owing in large part to the debt taken on to acquire the portion of Verizon Wireless previously owned by Vodafone (VOD). 
In other words, supply creates its own demand in world of bond indexes.
